<div class="ltx_page_main">

<div class="ltx_page_content">

# AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement

<div class="ltx_authors">

<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Libin Qiu </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zhirong Gao </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Junfu Chen </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yuhang Ye </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Weizhi Huang </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Xiaobo Xue </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Wenkai Qiu </span></span>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract">

###### Abstract

Large language model agents often fail to accumulate knowledge from
experience, treating each task as an independent challenge. Recent
methods extract experience as flattened textual knowledge, which cannot
capture procedural logic of complex subtasks. They also lack maintenance
mechanisms, causing repository degradation as experience accumulates. We
introduce AutoRefine, a framework that extracts and maintains dual-form
Experience Patterns from agent execution histories. For procedural
subtasks, we extract specialized subagents with independent reasoning
and memory. For static knowledge, we extract skill patterns as
guidelines or code snippets. A continuous maintenance mechanism scores,
prunes, and merges patterns to prevent repository degradation. Evaluated
on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and TravelPlanner, AutoRefine achieves 98.4%,
70.4%, and 27.1% respectively, with 20-73% step reductions. On
TravelPlanner, automatic extraction exceeds manually designed systems
(27.1% vs 12.1%), demonstrating its ability to capture procedural
coordination.

</div>

<div class="ltx_keywords">

Machine Learning, Large Language Models, Agent Learning

</div>

<div id="S1" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Autonomous agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have
demonstrated capabilities in completing tasks across various domains
such as web navigation, robotics, and household
assistance (Sarukkai<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib9" class="ltx_ref"
title="Self-generated in-context examples improve llm agents for sequential decision-making tasks">2025</a>;
Fu<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref"
title="Autoguide: automated generation and selection of context-aware guidelines for large language model agents">2024</a>;
Chen<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib11" class="ltx_ref"
title="Automanual: constructing instruction manuals by llm agents via interactive environmental learning">2024</a>).
However, unlike humans who autonomously build and update their
understanding through interaction, current agents often treat each new
task as an independent challenge. Each successfully completed task has
the potential to enrich the agent’s knowledge, enabling more reliable
performance on future similar tasks.

</div>

<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">

Recent research has explored enabling agents to learn from experience by
extracting knowledge from historical execution
traces (Fu<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref"
title="Autoguide: automated generation and selection of context-aware guidelines for large language model agents">2024</a>;
Chen<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib11" class="ltx_ref"
title="Automanual: constructing instruction manuals by llm agents via interactive environmental learning">2024</a>).
These methods face two primary challenges.

</div>

<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) Flattened
textual knowledge is insufficient for procedural logic.</span> Current
approaches represent experience as text, which cannot capture the
procedural logic of complex subtasks. For example, a subtask like “hotel
booking” involves sequential steps, conditional branching, and state
tracking—dynamic aspects that static text descriptions struggle to
represent.

</div>

<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) Lack of
experience maintenance mechanism.</span> These methods typically
incorporate all accumulated experience directly into the prompt, relying
on the LLM to select relevant knowledge. As experience grows, the prompt
becomes excessively long, burdening the context window and degrading
retrieval quality by failing to filter out obsolete or redundant
patterns.

</div>

<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">

To address these issues, we propose <span id="S1.p5.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AutoRefine</span>, a framework that
automatically extracts, maintains, and reuses <span id="S1.p5.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experience Patterns</span>. To address
the first challenge, we introduce <span id="S1.p5.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Subagent Pattern</span> extraction.
Instead of using flattened text, the framework identifies subtasks with
clear procedural logic (e.g., booking or reservation) and encapsulates
them as specialized subagents. These subagents maintain their own memory
and state management, enabling them to handle sequential reasoning and
error recovery autonomously. For general strategic knowledge that does
not require complex logic, we extract <span id="S1.p5.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Skill Patterns</span> as natural language
guidelines or code snippets. To address the second challenge, we
implement a <span id="S1.p5.1.5"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">continuous maintenance mechanism</span>.
Patterns are scored based on their empirical utility; low-quality
entries are pruned and redundant ones are merged. This dual-pattern
design with active maintenance ensures that the experience repository
remains compact, high-quality, and scalable.

</div>

<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">

We evaluate AutoRefine on three benchmarks: ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and
TravelPlanner. Experiments demonstrate three key findings. (1)
Dual-pattern automatic extraction is effective across diverse tasks:
98.4% on ALFWorld, 70.4% on ScienceWorld, and 27.1% on TravelPlanner,
with 20-73% step reductions. On TravelPlanner test set, our method
achieves 27.1%, substantially exceeding AutoManual (not reported) and
ATLAS (12.1%). (2) Automatic extraction matches manually designed
multi-agent systems without manual effort. On TravelPlanner test set,
our method (27.1%) more than doubles manually designed ATLAS (12.1%).
The advantage is most pronounced on commonsense constraints requiring
universal procedural patterns (37.90% vs 15.59%). (3) All three
components are necessary. Ablation on TravelPlanner validation set shows
removing subagents causes the largest drop (22.3%). Without maintenance,
repository size grows 4.5× and utilization degrades 8.9×. Without batch
extraction, performance drops 17.3%.

</div>

<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- <span id="S1.I1.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  We propose AutoRefine, a framework that automatically extracts and
  maintains dual-form Experience Patterns (skills and subagents) with
  continuous maintenance.

  </div>
- <span id="S1.I1.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  We introduce automatic subagent extraction that encapsulates
  procedural subtasks with independent reasoning and state management.

  </div>
- <span id="S1.I1.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  Experiments demonstrate strong performance across three benchmarks,
  with automatic extraction exceeding manual design on TravelPlanner
  (27.1% vs 12.1%).

  </div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work

<div id="S2.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Learning Paradigms for Agent Improvement

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Existing approaches to agent improvement can be categorized by their
learning paradigm.

</div>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Training-Based Methods.

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Reinforcement learning methods (Bai<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib39" class="ltx_ref"
title="Training a helpful and harmless assistant with reinforcement learning from human feedback">2022</a>;
Rafailov<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib40" class="ltx_ref"
title="Direct preference optimization: your language model is secretly a reward model">2023</a>;
Jaech<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib41" class="ltx_ref"
title="Openai o1 system card">2024</a>;
Guo<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib42" class="ltx_ref"
title="Deepseek-r1: incentivizing reasoning capability in llms via reinforcement learning">2025</a>)
optimize agent behavior through reward signals and gradient updates.
Fine-tuning approaches optimize model weights on domain-specific data.
These methods require substantial computational resources for training
and access to large-scale demonstration data or human feedback, limiting
their applicability when such resources are unavailable or when
deploying agents across diverse domains without retraining.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### In-Context Learning with External Data.

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

In-context learning offers an alternative by augmenting prompts with
relevant experiences without modifying model weights. However, most
in-context methods rely on external sources of experience. Trajectory
bootstrapping (Sarukkai<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et
al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib9" class="ltx_ref"
title="Self-generated in-context examples improve llm agents for sequential decision-making tasks">2025</a>)
accumulates trajectories from human demonstrations or oracle policies.
DSPy (Khattab<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib43" class="ltx_ref"
title="Dspy: compiling declarative language model calls into self-improving pipelines">2023</a>)
optimizes prompts using annotated task examples. Prompt optimization
methods (Zhou<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib44" class="ltx_ref"
title="Large language models are human-level prompt engineers">2022</a>;
Yang<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib45" class="ltx_ref"
title="Large language models as optimizers">2023</a>;
<a href="#bib.bib46" class="ltx_ref"
title="PromptAgent: strategic planning with language models enables expert-level prompt optimization">Wang<span
class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,</a> ) require collections
of successful examples to derive effective instructions. These
approaches depend on the availability and quality of external data,
limiting their applicability when such data is scarce or expensive to
obtain.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### In-Context Learning with Self-Generated Experience.

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

Some methods explore self-generated experience. Generative Agents
(Park<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib50" class="ltx_ref"
title="Generative agents: interactive simulacra of human behavior">2023</a>)
maintains episodic memories from agent interactions but focuses on
social simulation rather than task completion. CLIN
(Majumder<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib47" class="ltx_ref"
title="CLIN: a continually learning language agent for rapid task adaptation and generalization">2024</a>)
updates memory through causal abstractions from agent trials. RAP
(<a href="#bib.bib48" class="ltx_ref"
title="RAP: retrieval-augmented planning with contextual memory for multimodal llm agents">Kagaya<span
class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,</a> ) retrieves past
experiences from the agent’s own history. MemGPT
(Packer<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib49" class="ltx_ref"
title="MemGPT: towards llms as operating systems.">2023</a>) manages
memory through selective retention across episodes. These methods
accumulate experience from the agent’s own executions, yet they store
raw trajectories or episodic memories without distilling reusable
procedural knowledge or maintaining experience quality over time. Our
approach builds upon self-generated experience by introducing subagent
patterns and maintenance mechanisms.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Knowledge Extraction from Agent Experience

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

LLM-based agents have demonstrated capabilities in sequential
decision-making across web navigation
(Yao<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib15" class="ltx_ref"
title="React: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models">2022</a>;
<a href="#bib.bib23" class="ltx_ref"
title="WebArena: a realistic web environment for building autonomous agents">Zhou<span
class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,</a> ), embodied
environments (Shridhar<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et
al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib17" class="ltx_ref"
title="Alfworld: aligning text and embodied environments for interactive learning">2020</a>;
Zitkovich<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib24" class="ltx_ref"
title="Rt-2: vision-language-action models transfer web knowledge to robotic control">2023</a>),
and game playing (<a href="#bib.bib25" class="ltx_ref"
title="Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models">Wang<span
class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,</a> ;
Park<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib50" class="ltx_ref"
title="Generative agents: interactive simulacra of human behavior">2023</a>;
Zhu<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib26" class="ltx_ref"
title="Ghost in the minecraft: generally capable agents for open-world environments via large language models with text-based knowledge and memory">2023</a>).
These agents employ various reasoning strategies including
chain-of-thought prompting (Wei<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et
al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib27" class="ltx_ref"
title="Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models">2022</a>),
tool manipulation (<a href="#bib.bib28" class="ltx_ref"
title="ToolLLM: facilitating large language models to master 16000+ real-world apis">Qin<span
class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,</a> ;
Patil<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib29" class="ltx_ref"
title="Gorilla: large language model connected with massive apis">2024</a>;
Schick<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib30" class="ltx_ref"
title="Toolformer: language models can teach themselves to use tools">2023</a>),
and code generation (<a href="#bib.bib31" class="ltx_ref"
title="Code as policies: language model programs for embodied control">Liang<span
class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,</a> ;
Singh<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib32" class="ltx_ref"
title="Progprompt: generating situated robot task plans using large language models">2022</a>).
A key challenge is enabling agents to accumulate transferable knowledge
across tasks.

</div>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Self-Reflection and Feedback.

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Reflexion (Shinn<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib16" class="ltx_ref"
title="Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning">2023</a>)
reflects on failures and revises plans within a single task. Self-Refine
(Madaan<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib33" class="ltx_ref"
title="Self-refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback">2023</a>)
and RCI (Kim<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib34" class="ltx_ref"
title="Language models can solve computer tasks">2023</a>) incorporate
feedback iteratively to improve predictions. Tree-of-Thoughts
(Yao<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib35" class="ltx_ref"
title="Tree of thoughts: deliberate problem solving with large language models">2023</a>)
and related methods (<a href="#bib.bib36" class="ltx_ref"
title="Agent-pro: learning to evolve via policy-level reflection and optimization">Zhang<span
class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,</a> ;
Zhou<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib37" class="ltx_ref"
title="Language agent tree search unifies reasoning, acting, and planning in language models">2024</a>)
employ tree search with reflection to explore solution spaces. While
effective for single-episode adaptation, these methods do not accumulate
cross-task knowledge.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Experience as Textual Knowledge.

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Several approaches extract reusable knowledge from execution histories.
ExpeL (Zhao<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib12" class="ltx_ref"
title="Expel: llm agents are experiential learners">2024</a>) derives
task-level insights from successful trajectories. AutoGuide
(Fu<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref"
title="Autoguide: automated generation and selection of context-aware guidelines for large language model agents">2024</a>)
generates context-aware guidelines through contrastive analysis of
success-failure pairs, then retrieves relevant guidelines via semantic
similarity at test time. Voyager (<a href="#bib.bib25" class="ltx_ref"
title="Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models">Wang<span
class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,</a> ) and AdaPlanner
(Sun<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib13" class="ltx_ref"
title="Adaplanner: adaptive planning from feedback with language models">2023</a>)
store successful programs as skills for future tasks. AutoManual
(Chen<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib11" class="ltx_ref"
title="Automanual: constructing instruction manuals by llm agents via interactive environmental learning">2024</a>)
continually updates rules through interactive learning, categorizing
environmental knowledge into structured rule types. These methods
represent experience as textual descriptions. Such representations
struggle to capture procedural logic of complex multi-step subtasks
requiring sequential coordination, conditional branching, and state
management.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methodology

<div id="S3.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Problem Formulation

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We formalize the agent learning problem in a domain $`\mathcal{D}`$ as
follows. The agent receives a sequence of tasks
$`\{t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{N}\}`$ from domain $`\mathcal{D}`$, where each
task $`t_{i}`$ is specified by a natural language description and can be
solved via a sequence of actions $`\mathcal{A}`$. Upon completing task
$`t_{i}`$, the agent receives feedback
$`f_{i}\in\{\text{success},\text{failure}\}`$. The agent’s execution
produces a trajectory
$`\tau_{i}=\langle s_{0},a_{1},o_{1},s_{1},\ldots,a_{T},o_{T},s_{T}\rangle`$,
where $`s_{t}`$ denotes states, $`a_{t}`$ denotes actions, and $`o_{t}`$
denotes observations.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Pattern Repository.

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We denote the pattern repository as
$`\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{M}\}`$, where each pattern
$`p_{j}`$ can take one of two forms:

- <span id="S3.I1.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Skill
  Pattern</span>: Procedural knowledge expressed as natural language
  guidelines or executable code snippets that encapsulate successful
  strategies for handling specific task scenarios.

  </div>
- <span id="S3.I1.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Subagent
  Pattern</span>: Specialized agents that encapsulate specific
  intermediate steps or subtask solutions. Subagents maintain their own
  memory and reasoning capabilities, enabling them to handle complex
  procedural steps independently while reducing the cognitive load on
  the main agent.

  </div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Pattern Metadata.

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Each pattern $`p_{j}`$ is associated with metadata
$`m_{j}=(d_{j},c_{j},r_{j},u_{j},s_{j},e_{j})`$, where $`d_{j}`$ is a
brief description of the pattern, $`c_{j}`$ specifies the applicable
context, $`r_{j}`$ is the number of times the pattern was retrieved,
$`u_{j}`$ is the number of times it was actually used, $`s_{j}`$ is the
number of successful uses, and $`e_{j}`$ is the dense embedding vector
for similarity-based retrieval.

</div>

<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="/html/2601.22758/assets/x1.png" id="S3.F1.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="627"
height="323" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F1.2.1.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span
id="S3.F1.3.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of
AutoRefine framework with three stages: task execution, pattern
extraction, and pattern maintenance.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Framework Overview

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

We present an overview of our framework in
Figure <a href="#S3.F1" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 1 ‣ Pattern Metadata. ‣ 3.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. The framework consists of
three stages: (1) Task Execution (§<a href="#S3.SS3" class="ltx_ref"
title="3.3 Task Execution with Patterns ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>): the agent retrieves
relevant patterns via semantic similarity and uses them as contextual
guidance during execution; (2) Pattern Extraction
(§<a href="#S3.SS4" class="ltx_ref"
title="3.4 Pattern Extraction from Trajectories ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>): after every $`K`$ tasks, a
specialized agent performs contrastive analysis between successful and
failed trajectories to extract new patterns; (3) Pattern Maintenance
(§<a href="#S3.SS5" class="ltx_ref"
title="3.5 Pattern Maintenance ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>): at exponentially spaced
intervals, the framework scores, prunes, and merges patterns to maintain
repository quality.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Task Execution with Patterns

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">

For each incoming task $`t_{i}`$, the agent performs pattern-augmented
execution through three coordinated steps: pattern retrieval, pattern
integration, and metadata tracking.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Pattern Retrieval.

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Given task $`t_{i}`$ with description $`d_{\text{task}}`$, we retrieve
patterns whose contexts are semantically similar to the task
requirements. For comprehensive pattern discovery, we first instruct the
LLM to generate multiple retrieval queries
$`\{q_{1},q_{2},\ldots,q_{m}\}`$ that reformulate $`d_{\text{task}}`$
from different perspectives. We subsequently compute semantic similarity
between each query and pattern context using cosine similarity over
embedding vectors generated by
Qwen3-Embedding-4B (Zhang<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et
al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib21" class="ltx_ref"
title="Qwen3 embedding: advancing text embedding and reranking through foundation models">2025</a>).
The final similarity score for pattern $`p_{j}`$ is the maximum across
all queries:
$`\text{sim}(t_{i},p_{j})=\max_{i}\text{sim}(q_{i},p_{j})`$. We rank all
patterns by their similarity scores and retrieve the top-$`k`$ patterns
above threshold $`\theta`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | 
``` math
\mathcal{P}_{\text{retrieved}}=\text{TopK}\left(\{p_{j}\in\mathcal{P}:\text{sim}(t_{i},p_{j})\geq\theta\},k\right)
``` |  |

To prevent retrieving multiple similar patterns, we optionally apply
maximal marginal relevance (MMR), which balances relevance and diversity
through score.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | 
``` math
\text{MMR}(p_{j})=\lambda\cdot\text{sim}(t_{i},p_{j})-(1-\lambda)\cdot\max_{p_{k}\in\mathcal{P}_{\text{selected}}}\text{sim}(p_{j},p_{k})
``` |  |

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Pattern Integration.

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

During execution, the agent incorporates retrieved patterns as
contextual guidance. We accommodate two pattern types: skills and
subagents. Skill patterns encoded as natural language guidelines are
incorporated by augmenting the agent’s system prompt with pattern
descriptions and procedural steps. For executable code snippets, we
register them as callable tools in the agent’s action space, allowing
direct invocation (e.g., <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">validate_data(input)</span>).
Subagent patterns encapsulate complex multi-step procedures with
internal state. We adopt hierarchical delegation: the main agent
identifies subtasks matching a subagent’s specialization via semantic
similarity, transfers relevant context, and delegates execution. The
subagent operates independently with its own memory, returning results
upon completion. This decomposition reduces the main agent’s reasoning
complexity by abstracting complex procedures into atomic operations.
Concrete examples of skill and subagent patterns are provided in
Appendix <a href="#A4" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix D Experiment Pattern Examples ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Metadata Tracking.

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

During execution, we maintain pattern metadata
$`m_{j}=(d_{j},c_{j},r_{j},u_{j},s_{j},e_{j})`$ to track pattern quality
and usage statistics. For each pattern
$`p_{j}\in\mathcal{P}_{\text{retrieved}}`$, we increment retrieval count
$`r_{j}`$. Given that not all retrieved patterns are necessarily
adopted, we use a dedicated agent to verify actual invocation and
increment utilization count $`u_{j}`$ accordingly. For tasks resulting
in $`f_{i}=\text{success}`$, we increment success count $`s_{j}`$. This
metadata directly informs subsequent maintenance operations
(§<a href="#S3.SS5" class="ltx_ref"
title="3.5 Pattern Maintenance ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>), where patterns are scored,
pruned, and merged based on their empirical contribution.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS4" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Pattern Extraction from Trajectories

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">

Pattern extraction distills reusable knowledge from execution
experience, forming the core learning mechanism of our framework.
Inspired by batch updates in reinforcement learning (Barto,
<a href="#bib.bib22" class="ltx_ref"
title="Reinforcement learning: an introduction. by richard’s sutton">2021</a>),
we extract patterns from batches of trajectories rather than individual
task executions, which identifies generalizable strategies through
cross-trajectory analysis.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Batch Extraction Strategy.

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We perform extraction every $`K`$ tasks (default $`K=10`$) over the
recent trajectory set
$`\mathcal{H}_{\text{recent}}=\{(\tau_{i},f_{i}):i>n-K\}`$, which
contains both successful ($`f_{i}=1`$) and failed ($`f_{i}=0`$)
executions. Recurring patterns in successful trajectories indicate
generalizable strategies, while their absence in failures offers
contrastive evidence. Batch-level extraction mitigates overfitting to
task-specific details that would occur in single-task extraction. We
consider sparse-reward environments where task outcome
$`f_{i}\in\{0,1\}`$ is determined at episode termination, following
prior work (Fu<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref"
title="Autoguide: automated generation and selection of context-aware guidelines for large language model agents">2024</a>;
Zhao<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib12" class="ltx_ref"
title="Expel: llm agents are experiential learners">2024</a>).

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Agent-Driven Extraction Pipeline.

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Pattern extraction is conducted by a specialized extraction agent
$`\mathcal{A}_{\text{extract}}`$ that autonomously extracts reusable
knowledge from trajectory batches. Given the recent trajectories
$`\mathcal{H}_{\text{recent}}`$ partitioned into successes
$`\mathcal{H}^{+}=\{(\tau_{i},1)\}`$ and failures
$`\mathcal{H}^{-}=\{(\tau_{i},0)\}`$, we design prompts that guide the
agent to conduct contrastive analysis and pattern abstraction. The agent
examines execution trajectories to identify recurring action sequences
and decision strategies that differentiate successful outcomes from
failures. The agent compares trajectories where executions diverge,
contrasting actions that lead to success versus those resulting in
failure. Through this contrastive analysis, the agent generates natural
language explanations that elucidate the underlying causal principles.
These explanations clarify why certain strategies succeed while others
fail, forming the foundation of extracted patterns.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">

The agent subsequently abstracts these explanations and identified
strategies into structured patterns with complete metadata
$`m_{p}=(d_{p},c_{p},0,0,0,e_{p})`$, where $`d_{p}`$ encapsulates a
description of the pattern, $`c_{p}`$ specifies applicability contexts,
usage statistics $`(r_{p},u_{p},s_{p})`$ are initialized to zero, and
$`e_{p}=\text{Embed}(c_{p})`$ is the embedding vector for semantic
retrieval. The agent determines pattern type based on complexity: simple
procedural guidelines or code snippets become
<span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">skill
patterns</span>, while multi-step procedures requiring sustained
reasoning become <span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3.5.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">subagent patterns</span>. The complete
prompt templates that guide the extraction agent through this process
are detailed in Appendix <a href="#A5" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix E Pattern Extraction Prompts ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS5" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Pattern Maintenance

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">

Without periodic maintenance, the pattern repository $`\mathcal{P}`$
accumulates outdated and redundant entries, resulting in retrieval
inefficiency and degraded pattern quality.
Following (Sarukkai<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib9" class="ltx_ref"
title="Self-generated in-context examples improve llm agents for sequential decision-making tasks">2025</a>),
we perform maintenance at exponentially spaced intervals
$`(n_{\text{threshold}}=10,20,40,80,\ldots)`$. This schedule balances
two objectives: early intervals remove unstable patterns when usage
statistics are sparse; later intervals reduce computational overhead as
the repository stabilizes.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Pattern Scoring and Pruning.

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

At each maintenance event, we compute a utility score for each pattern
based on metadata statistics. The score integrates three
terms—effectiveness (success rate), frequency (usage count), and
precision (utilization ratio):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | 
``` math
\text{score}(p_{j})=\underbrace{\frac{s_{j}}{u_{j}+\epsilon}}_{\text{effectiveness}}\cdot\underbrace{\log(1+u_{j})}_{\text{frequency}}\cdot\underbrace{\left(1+\frac{u_{j}}{r_{j}+\epsilon}\right)}_{\text{precision}}
``` |  | <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span> |

where $`\epsilon=0.01`$ ensures numerical stability. The effectiveness
term $`s_{j}/(u_{j}+\epsilon)`$ quantifies contribution to task success.
The frequency term $`\log(1+u_{j})`$ incentivizes usage while precluding
dominance through logarithmic scaling. The precision term
$`(1+u_{j}/(r_{j}+\epsilon))`$ reflects retrieval relevance: high ratios
indicate retrieved patterns are actually utilized, reflecting
well-specified contexts. After scoring, we remove the bottom $`\alpha`$
percentile ($`\alpha=20\%`$) to eliminate low-utility patterns while
retaining the effective majority.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Pattern Merging.

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

To eliminate redundancy, we merge similar patterns through a two-stage
process. First, we perform similarity-based filtering: pattern pairs
$`(p_{i},p_{j})`$ with matching types (both skills or both subagents)
and high embedding similarity are identified as merge candidates:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | 
``` math
\small\mathcal{C}=\{(p_{i},p_{j})|\text{sim}(e_{i},e_{j})\geq\theta_{\text{merge}}\land\text{type}(p_{i})=\text{type}(p_{j})\}
``` |  | <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span> |

where $`\theta_{\text{merge}}=0.85`$ and $`e_{i},e_{j}`$ are embeddings
from pattern metadata. This filtering uses vector similarity over
descriptions $`d_{i},d_{j}`$ and contexts $`c_{i},c_{j}`$ to reduce
computational cost.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">

Second, for each candidate pair in $`\mathcal{C}`$, we deploy a merge
agent $`\mathcal{A}_{\text{merge}}`$ to determine whether merging is
warranted by analyzing: (1) whether both patterns address the same
subtask, (2) whether their procedural steps are compatible, (3) whether
their applicability contexts overlap. If confirmed, we construct
$`p_{\text{merged}}`$ with agent-synthesized description
$`d_{\text{merged}}`$ and context $`c_{\text{merged}}`$, and recompute
embedding $`e_{\text{merged}}`$ accordingly. Usage statistics are
aggregated: $`r_{\text{merged}}=r_{i}+r_{j}`$,
$`u_{\text{merged}}=u_{i}+u_{j}`$, $`s_{\text{merged}}=s_{i}+s_{j}`$.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">

We apply agglomerative clustering: iteratively merge the most similar
pair in $`\mathcal{C}`$ until no candidates remain.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments

<div id="S4.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Benchmarks.

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We evaluate on three representative domains requiring sequential
decision-making and procedural knowledge:
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ALFWorld</span> (Shridhar<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib17" class="ltx_ref"
title="Alfworld: aligning text and embodied environments for interactive learning">2020</a>)
is a text-based interactive environment simulating household tasks
(e.g., “put a clean mug in the coffee machine”), using the standard
split with 134 training and 140 test tasks across 6 task types.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ScienceWorld</span> (Wang<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib18" class="ltx_ref"
title="ScienceWorld: is your agent smarter than a 5th grader?">2022</a>)
is a science experiment simulation requiring multi-step reasoning,
focusing on 30 tasks from the “boil” and “grow” categories.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TravelPlanner</span> (Xie<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib19" class="ltx_ref"
title="TravelPlanner: a benchmark for real-world planning with language agents">2024</a>)
is a comprehensive travel planning benchmark requiring multi-agent
coordination for complex itinerary generation with 3-7 day trip planning
involving multiple constraints, evaluated on 180 validation and 1000
test scenarios.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Baselines.

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

We compare against recent experience learning methods, prompt-based
baselines, and specialized multi-agent frameworks:
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ReAct</span> (Yao<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib15" class="ltx_ref"
title="React: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models">2022</a>)
prompts the LLM to generate reasoning traces and actions, without
learning from experience. <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reflexion</span> (Shinn<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib16" class="ltx_ref"
title="Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning">2023</a>)
generates verbal reflections from failed trajectories and stores them in
episodic memory for retrieval. Following the original work, Reflexion
agents are allowed to try at most 3 trials for each task.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ReAct +
Reflexion</span> combines ReAct’s reasoning approach with Reflexion’s
self-reflection mechanism for improved performance. For
ALFWorld-specific comparisons (Table <a href="#S4.T2" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 2 ‣ Detailed ALFWorld Performance. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), we additionally include
results from <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ExpeL</span> (Zhao<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib12" class="ltx_ref"
title="Expel: llm agents are experiential learners">2024</a>), which
extracts task-level insights from successful trajectories,
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AdaPlanner</span> (Sun<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib13" class="ltx_ref"
title="Adaplanner: adaptive planning from feedback with language models">2023</a>),
which generates and adaptively refines code-style plans with skill
memory, and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.6"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AutoManual</span> (Chen<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib11" class="ltx_ref"
title="Automanual: constructing instruction manuals by llm agents via interactive environmental learning">2024</a>),
an online learning framework with Planner-Builder-Formulator
architecture. We also plan to compare with
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.7"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AutoGuide</span> (Fu<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref"
title="Autoguide: automated generation and selection of context-aware guidelines for large language model agents">2024</a>),
which generates conditional guidelines from offline demonstrations.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.8"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ATLAS</span> (Choi<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib14" class="ltx_ref"
title="ATLAS: constraints-aware multi-agent collaboration for real-world travel planning">2025</a>)
is Google’s multi-agent framework with manually designed specialized
agents for travel planning, used specifically for TravelPlanner
benchmark comparison.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">

Unless otherwise specified, all methods use Claude-sonnet-4 as the base
LLM with temperature 0.7. For the ALFWorld subtask comparison
(Table <a href="#S4.T2" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 2 ‣ Detailed ALFWorld Performance. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), to ensure fair comparison
with prior work, all methods including ours use GPT-4-turbo.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">

All results are averaged over 3 random seeds with different task
orderings. We report mean and standard deviation, with statistical
significance tested via paired t-test ($`p<0.05`$). Implementation
details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" class="ltx_ref"
title="B.2 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix B Details of Experimental Setup ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Main Results

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Our framework achieves the highest success rates across all domains:
+2.9% in ALFWorld, +1.2% in ScienceWorld, and +18.0% in TravelPlanner
over ReAct + Reflexion (Table <a href="#S4.T1" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 1 ‣ Baselines. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Step reductions correlate
with task difficulty.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">

Compared to ReAct + Reflexion, our method reduces steps by 20.5% in
ALFWorld (12.8 vs. 16.1), 59.0% in ScienceWorld (16.5 vs. 40.2), and
72.8% in TravelPlanner (21.8 vs. 80.2). This pattern aligns with task
difficulty: in TravelPlanner where success rates are low (8-10%),
Reflexion requires 77.9 steps and ReAct+Reflexion 80.2 steps—3.6× and
3.7× our method respectively. Across benchmarks, moving from
high-success ALFWorld (95%+ SR) to low-success TravelPlanner, Reflexion
steps increase 5.0× (15.7 → 77.9) while ours increase 1.7× (12.8 →
21.8). This difference arises from distinct mechanisms: our pattern
repository provides procedural knowledge extracted from prior successful
experiences, while reflection-based methods iterate through
fail-reflect-retry cycles that accumulate steps when tasks frequently
fail. The dual-pattern design enables direct guidance through skills and
procedural encapsulation through subagents.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Detailed ALFWorld Performance.

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Table <a href="#S4.T2" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 2 ‣ Detailed ALFWorld Performance. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> presents breakdown across six
ALFWorld subtasks. Our zero-shot approach achieves 97.0% overall success
rate, 0.4% below AutoManual (97.4%) which uses one manually crafted
skill example. On simple tasks (Put, Heat, Examine), both methods
achieve 100.0%. On complex multi-step tasks (Put Two), AutoManual
achieves 90.2% while our method achieves 88.2%. Compared to methods
using more examples—ExpeL (12 examples, 79.2%) and AdaPlanner (6
examples, 76.4%)—our automatic extraction from task experiences achieves
higher success rates without manual design. Additionally, we evaluate
subagent extraction on TravelPlanner (§<a href="#S4.SS4" class="ltx_ref"
title="4.4 Subagent Extraction Performance on Complex Multi-Agent Tasks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>).

</div>

<div id="S4.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Ablation Study

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">

We evaluate the contribution of three key components—subagents, batch
extraction, and maintenance—on TravelPlanner validation set (180 tasks).
This ablation tests our core claim: dual-pattern design with subagents
is necessary for complex tasks, and pattern quality depends on both
batch extraction for generalization and maintenance for preventing
repository degradation.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Subagents (<span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">w/o Subagents</span>).

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

This experiment evaluates whether subagent extraction (our core
contribution) is necessary for complex procedural tasks. Removing
subagent patterns causes the largest performance drop (35.6%
$`\rightarrow`$ 13.3%), with worst performance across all constraint
categories (Figure <a href="#S4.F2" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 2 ‣ Maintenance (w/o Maintenance). ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). The drop is more pronounced
on commonsense constraints (54.4% $`\rightarrow`$ 23.3%, 57% relative
decrease) than hard constraints (38.9% $`\rightarrow`$ 29.4%, 24%
relative decrease).

</div>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">

This pattern aligns with Finding 3 in §<a href="#S4.SS4" class="ltx_ref"
title="4.4 Subagent Extraction Performance on Complex Multi-Agent Tasks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>: automatically extracted
subagents excel at capturing universal procedural patterns that
generalize across cases. On TravelPlanner, using only skill patterns
forces the main agent to handle procedural multi-step coordination
(e.g., accommodation-dining-attraction searches with temporal and budget
constraints) within a single reasoning context. As context length grows,
relevant coordination constraints from previous tasks may be lost.
Automatic subagent extraction encapsulates these coordination procedures
with internal state and independent reasoning, allowing direct reuse
across tasks.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Batch Extraction (<span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">w/o Batch Extraction</span>).

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

This experiment evaluates whether batch-level contrastive analysis
(§<a href="#S3.SS4" class="ltx_ref"
title="3.4 Pattern Extraction from Trajectories ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>) improves pattern
generalization compared to single-task extraction. Observation:
single-task extraction reduces final pass rate significantly (35.6%
$`\rightarrow`$ 18.3%), with performance drops across all categories in
Figure <a href="#S4.F2" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 2 ‣ Maintenance (w/o Maintenance). ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> exceeding those from removing
maintenance. Figure <a href="#S4.F3" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 3 ‣ Maintenance (w/o Maintenance). ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(a) shows repository grows to
58 patterns (2.4× full model). More patterns but worse performance
indicates extracted patterns overfit to task-specific details.
Figure <a href="#S4.F3" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 3 ‣ Maintenance (w/o Maintenance). ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(b) shows utilization drops
from 0.71 to 0.28 and the trend resembles the no-maintenance variant,
though less severe. However, the performance degradation in
Figure <a href="#S4.F2" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 2 ‣ Maintenance (w/o Maintenance). ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> is more pronounced than
no-maintenance because patterns extracted from single tasks lack
generalization. Batch extraction with contrastive analysis identifies
strategies recurring across multiple successful trajectories while
absent in failures, producing patterns that generalize to new tasks.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Maintenance (<span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">w/o Maintenance</span>).

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

This experiment evaluates whether periodic pruning and merging
(§<a href="#S3.SS5" class="ltx_ref"
title="3.5 Pattern Maintenance ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>) prevents repository
degradation. Observation: removing maintenance reduces final pass rate
(35.6% $`\rightarrow`$ 31.1%). Figure <a href="#S4.F3" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 3 ‣ Maintenance (w/o Maintenance). ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(a) shows repository size grows
linearly to 108 patterns (4.5× full model).
Figure <a href="#S4.F3" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 3 ‣ Maintenance (w/o Maintenance). ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(b) shows utilization rate
starts at 0.68 but drops rapidly to 0.08 as tasks accumulate, indicating
most retrieved patterns are not used. Interestingly, hard constraint
performance (44.4%) slightly exceeds full model (38.9%), likely because
the larger repository occasionally retrieves case-specific patterns
useful for explicit requirements. However, the overall performance drop
and 8.9× utilization degradation (0.71 $`\rightarrow`$ 0.08) confirm
that maintenance is necessary to prevent accumulation of low-quality
patterns. The maintenance mechanism scores patterns by effectiveness,
frequency, and precision, then prunes the bottom 20% and merges similar
patterns.

</div>

<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="/html/2601.22758/assets/x2.png" id="S4.F2.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="789"
height="429" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F2.2.1.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span

results on TravelPlanner validation set. Subagent removal causes larger
drops on commonsense constraints (57% relative decrease) than hard
constraints (24% relative decrease).</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S4.SS4" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Subagent Extraction Performance on Complex Multi-Agent Tasks

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">

Table <a href="#S4.T3" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents performance
comparison on TravelPlanner test set. Our method achieves 27.1% final
pass rate, with Ours+ReAct reaching 34.10%. We analyze two key aspects:
comparison with manually designed agents and complementarity with
reflection-based methods.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Automatic Pattern Extraction vs. Manual Multi-Agent Design.

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Compared to manually designed ATLAS, our method outperforms on
commonsense constraints (Macro: 37.9% vs. 15.59%) but underperforms on
hard constraints (Macro: 32.60% vs. 33.56%). For commonsense
constraints, consider transportation mode consistency in validation case
idx=90: when no suitable flights satisfy round-trip conditions and the
agent travels via self-driving or taxi, the return trip cannot use
flights either. Our pattern extraction identifies such universal rules
from successful trajectories and transfers them to new cases. For hard
constraints, case idx=121 requires diverse dinner cuisines (Indian,
Chinese, Mediterranean, American) within a \$2300 budget with
pet-friendly accommodations. Each case has distinct requirements.
Manually designed agents can encode explicit verification logic for each
constraint type, while automatically extracted patterns struggle with
such case-specific scenarios.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Complementary Benefits of Experience and Reflection.

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Our method achieves 37.9% macro pass rate on commonsense constraints, a
21.4 percentage point improvement over ReAct (16.5%). However, ReAct
achieves 39.1% on hard constraints, exceeding our method (32.6%) and
ATLAS (33.56%). Hard constraints appear explicitly in task descriptions.
For example, case idx=122 specifies entire room rental with no
self-driving travel. ReAct can directly parse and verify such explicit
requirements without prior experience.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">

Combining both approaches yields substantial improvements. Ours+ReAct
achieves 34.10% final pass rate, compared to 27.10% (Ours) and 10.40%
(ReAct). Performance gains are consistent across constraint types:
commonsense increases by 4.3 points (37.9% → 42.2%), hard constraints by
4.6 points (32.6% → 37.2%). Cross-task pattern accumulation and
within-task reflection operate on complementary dimensions: experience
provides transferable procedural knowledge, while reflection handles
task-specific verification.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span>

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">

We presented AutoRefine, a framework that extracts and maintains
Experience Patterns from agent execution histories. These patterns
capture generalizable procedural knowledge from successful executions.
AutoRefine addresses limitations of existing methods through
dual-pattern extraction and continuous maintenance. For procedural
subtasks, we extract specialized subagents with independent reasoning.
For static knowledge, we extract skill patterns as guidelines or code
snippets. The maintenance mechanism scores, prunes, and merges patterns
to prevent repository degradation. Experiments on ALFWorld,
ScienceWorld, and TravelPlanner demonstrate that AutoRefine achieves
strong performance with 20-73% step reductions. On TravelPlanner,
automatic extraction exceeds manually designed systems (27.1% vs 12.1%).
Future work includes extending the framework to learn from failures and
exploring transfer across task domains.

</div>

</div>
