<div id="A1" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Additional Discussions

<div id="A1.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Difference with Prior Methods

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We compare AutoRefine with prior methods that extract knowledge from
agent experiences, i.e., ExpeL (Zhao<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">
et al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib12" class="ltx_ref"
title="Expel: llm agents are experiential learners">2024</a>),
AutoGuide (Fu<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref"
title="Autoguide: automated generation and selection of context-aware guidelines for large language model agents">2024</a>),
and AutoManual (Chen<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib11" class="ltx_ref"
title="Automanual: constructing instruction manuals by llm agents via interactive environmental learning">2024</a>),
and discuss all differences here:

</div>

<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1) Pattern
Representation Form.</span> ExpeL extracts task-level insights as
natural language summaries. AutoGuide generates conditional guidelines
in text format. AutoManual constructs structured rule systems with six
rule types. All prior methods represent experience using single-form
representations—either text rules or code skills. In contrast, our
framework employs dual-form patterns: <span id="A1.SS1.p2.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Skill Patterns</span> (guidelines or
code snippets) for simple procedural knowledge, and
<span id="A1.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Subagent
Patterns</span> (specialized agents with independent reasoning and
memory) for complex multi-step subtasks. This dual-form design enables
us to capture both lightweight strategies and procedural logic requiring
sustained state management. As demonstrated in
§<a href="#S4.SS4" class="ltx_ref"
title="4.4 Subagent Extraction Performance on Complex Multi-Agent Tasks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>, subagent patterns achieve
100% constraint satisfaction on transportation mode consistency by
maintaining state across multi-step searches, while text-based
representations struggle with such procedural coordination.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2) Extraction
Strategy.</span> ExpeL and AutoGuide extract patterns offline from
collected trajectories after task completion. AutoManual performs online
extraction but processes single tasks individually. Our framework
extracts patterns every $`K`$ tasks (default $`K=10`$) using contrastive
analysis between successful and failed trajectories. Recurring patterns
across multiple successes indicate generalizable strategies; contrasting
with failures identifies causal principles rather than spurious
correlations. Ablation results (§4) show that removing batch extraction
reduces performance by 17.3%, with repository size growing 2.4× due to
task-specific overfitting.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3) Pattern
Retrieval Mechanism.</span> ExpeL and AutoGuide retrieve relevant
patterns via semantic similarity between pattern contexts and task
descriptions. AutoManual incorporates all accumulated rules directly
into the prompt without selective retrieval, relying on the LLM to
identify relevant rules. This approach does not scale: as AutoManual
acknowledges, their repository contains only 6 rule types with examples,
whereas pattern repositories in realistic settings accumulate hundreds
of entries. Our framework employs multi-query retrieval: the LLM
generates multiple reformulations of the task description from different
perspectives (e.g., “transportation planning,” “budget optimization,”
“constraint satisfaction”), then retrieves patterns whose contexts match
any query above threshold $`\theta`$. We further apply Maximal Marginal
Relevance (MMR) to balance relevance and diversity, preventing retrieval
of multiple similar patterns. This retrieval mechanism maintains
efficiency as repository size scales.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">4) Maintenance
Mechanism.</span> ExpeL and AutoGuide perform score-based deletion:
patterns with low scores are removed periodically. However, as
AutoManual observes, LLM-assigned scores are often unreliable due to
overconfidence. AutoManual employs a Consolidator agent to merge
redundant rules, but still relies on score-based pruning. Our
maintenance mechanism addresses both scoring unreliability and
redundancy through three components: (i) <span id="A1.SS1.p5.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">empirical utility scoring</span> based
on usage statistics rather than LLM judgments—effectiveness (success
rate), frequency (usage count), and precision (utilization ratio); (ii)
<span id="A1.SS1.p5.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">percentile-based pruning</span> removes
bottom 20% rather than absolute thresholds, adapting to repository
quality distribution; (iii) <span id="A1.SS1.p5.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">agent-verified merging</span> uses
similarity-based filtering followed by agent verification of semantic
equivalence, preventing incorrect merges. Ablation results show that
without maintenance, repository size grows 4.5× and utilization rate
degrades 8.9× (0.71 $`\rightarrow`$ 0.08), demonstrating that active
quality control is necessary.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5) Pattern
Integration During Execution.</span> Prior methods augment the agent’s
prompt with retrieved patterns as textual context. Our framework
accommodates two integration mechanisms corresponding to our dual-form
patterns: (i) Skill patterns are integrated through prompt augmentation
(text guidelines) or tool registration (code snippets), similar to prior
work; (ii) Subagent patterns employ <span id="A1.SS1.p6.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hierarchical delegation</span>—the main
agent identifies subtasks matching a subagent’s specialization,
transfers relevant context, and delegates execution. The subagent
operates independently with its own memory and reasoning capability,
returning results upon subtask completion. This delegation reduces the
main agent’s cognitive complexity by abstracting complex procedural
coordination into atomic operations. For example, in TravelPlanner, the
main agent delegates the entire transportation planning subtask
(requiring 20+ tool calls with budget tracking and constraint
enforcement) to the Transportation Subagent, receiving only the final
plan. This contrasts with prior methods where the main agent must handle
all intermediate steps within its own reasoning context.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS1.p7.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">6) Metadata
Tracking.</span> ExpeL and AutoGuide track only pattern content and
score. AutoManual extends this with Type, Content, Example, and Logs
(application history). Our metadata system tracks six attributes:
description $`d_{j}`$, applicability context $`c_{j}`$, retrieval count
$`r_{j}`$, utilization count $`u_{j}`$, success count $`s_{j}`$, and
embedding vector $`e_{j}`$. Critically, we distinguish between
<span id="A1.SS1.p7.7.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">retrieval</span> (pattern was fetched
based on similarity) and <span id="A1.SS1.p7.7.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">utilization</span> (pattern was
actually invoked during execution). This distinction enables our scoring
formula to compute precision $`(1+u_{j}/(r_{j}+\epsilon))`$, which
quantifies whether retrieved patterns are genuinely useful. Patterns
with high retrieval but low utilization indicate poor context
specification or obsolete strategies, and are candidates for pruning.
This fine-grained tracking provides actionable signals for maintenance
operations, as evidenced by maintained utilization rate (0.71) compared
to no-maintenance baseline (0.08).

</div>

</div>

<div id="A1.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Limitations

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

AutoRefine has several limitations that warrant discussion.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pattern Type
Classification Accuracy.</span> The framework uses an LLM-based
classification agent to determine whether extracted strategies should
become skill patterns or subagent patterns
(§<a href="#S3.SS4" class="ltx_ref"
title="3.4 Pattern Extraction from Trajectories ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>,
Appendix <a href="#A5" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix E Pattern Extraction Prompts ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>). Our classification criteria
(statefulness, reasoning complexity, subtask completeness, cognitive
load) provide structured guidance, but misclassification can occur.
Simple procedures might be over-engineered as subagents, increasing
invocation overhead; conversely, complex coordination logic might be
under-specified as skills, failing to capture necessary state
management. In our experiments, we did not systematically evaluate
classification accuracy, relying instead on end-to-end task performance.
Future work could establish ground-truth labels for pattern types
through expert annotation or develop self-correction mechanisms where
patterns are reclassified based on utilization statistics.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Applicability
Context Precision.</span> Pattern retrieval depends on semantic
similarity between task descriptions and pattern contexts $`c_{j}`$.
While our contrastive extraction approach generates contexts by
analyzing where patterns succeed versus fail, these contexts may lack
precision. Overly broad contexts cause irrelevant patterns to be
retrieved (low precision in retrieval, though our scoring formula
penalizes unused patterns); overly narrow contexts cause useful patterns
to be missed (low recall). We partially address this through multi-query
retrieval and MMR diversity balancing, but context quality remains
dependent on the extraction agent’s ability to articulate applicability
conditions. Incorporating user feedback or active learning to refine
contexts based on retrieval-utilization mismatches could improve
precision.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS2.p4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hyperparameter
Sensitivity Across Domains.</span> Our maintenance mechanism uses fixed
hyperparameters: pruning percentile $`\alpha=20\%`$, merge threshold
$`\theta_{\text{merge}}=0.85`$, batch size $`K=10`$. While Appendix
provides sensitivity analysis showing these values are robust within
tested ranges, optimal settings may vary across domains. Environments
with high task diversity may benefit from larger $`K`$ to accumulate
diverse contrastive examples; environments with rapid knowledge
obsolescence may require more aggressive pruning ($`\alpha>20\%`$).
Currently, these hyperparameters must be set manually based on domain
characteristics. Developing adaptive mechanisms that adjust
hyperparameters based on repository growth rate, utilization trends, or
task distribution shifts would enhance robustness.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS2.p5.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cold Start
Problem.</span> Initially, the pattern repository $`\mathcal{P}`$ is
empty or contains only minimal seed patterns. During the first $`K`$
tasks, agents rely entirely on base LLM capabilities without pattern
guidance. Performance improves as patterns accumulate, but early tasks
may exhibit lower success rates compared to methods with human-designed
prior knowledge. In our experiments
(Figure <a href="#S4.F3" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 3 ‣ Maintenance (w/o Maintenance). ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), repository size stabilizes
after 40-60 tasks, suggesting a learning phase duration. For
time-critical applications, initializing the repository with seed
patterns from offline demonstrations or transfer learning from related
domains could accelerate convergence.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">

These limitations represent engineering trade-offs and domain-specific
challenges rather than fundamental flaws in our dual-pattern design or
maintenance mechanisms. The core contributions—subagent patterns for
procedural encapsulation, batch contrastive extraction for
generalization, and empirical utility-based maintenance—remain valid.
Future work addressing these limitations could enhance the framework’s
applicability across broader domains and deployment scenarios.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A1.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Broader Impacts

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">

The AutoRefine framework presents both benefits and risks that warrant
consideration.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Safety and
Reliability.</span> Automated pattern extraction reduces trial-and-error
behavior by reusing validated strategies, potentially minimizing errors
in deployed systems. However, incorrectly extracted patterns may encode
flawed strategies that propagate across future tasks. If the extraction
agent misidentifies correlation as causation during contrastive
analysis, resulting patterns could lead to systematically wrong
decisions. Pattern classification errors may cause agents to overlook
critical dependencies, leading to constraint violations.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Value for Human
Workers.</span> The patterns serve as interpretable documentation of
learned strategies. Skill patterns expressed as natural language or
code, and subagent patterns with explicit procedural logic, can aid
human workers in understanding task decomposition and requirements. For
example, subagent patterns document constraint enforcement rules that
novice planners might overlook. This representation provides
transparency into agent decision-making processes.

</div>

<div id="A1.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A1.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Potential for
Misuse.</span> Agents equipped with automatically extracted patterns for
harmful tasks (e.g., automated social engineering, spam generation)
could become more effective through accumulated experience. If execution
trajectories contain sensitive information, extracted patterns might
inadvertently encode and propagate such data. Deploying AutoRefine
requires careful consideration of task domains, trajectory data
governance, and pattern auditing mechanisms to prevent malicious use or
information leakage.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A2" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Details of Experimental Setup

<div id="A2.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Dataset Details

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### ALFWorld.

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

ALFWorld (Shridhar<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib17" class="ltx_ref"
title="Alfworld: aligning text and embodied environments for interactive learning">2020</a>)
is a text-based interactive environment that simulates household tasks
by aligning abstract TextWorld environments with embodied ALFRED tasks.
The benchmark contains 6 task types across 134 training and 140 test
scenarios:

- <span id="A2.I1.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pick &
  Place</span>: Pick up and place objects (e.g., “put a washed apple in
  the fridge”)

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I1.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1.1"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Clean</span>: Clean objects (e.g.,
  “clean a bowl and put it in the cupboard”)

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I1.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Heat</span>:
  Heat objects (e.g., “heat a potato with the microwave”)

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I1.i4"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cool</span>:
  Cool objects (e.g., “cool a tomato and put it in the fridge”)

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I1.i5"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i5.p1.1.1"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Examine</span>: Examine objects under
  light (e.g., “examine an alarm clock under a lamp”)

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I1.i6"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pick Two
  Objects</span>: More complex multi-object manipulation tasks

  </div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">

Tasks involve sequential decision-making with available actions
including navigation (<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">go to \[location\]</span>), object
manipulation (<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">take \[object\] from
\[receptacle\]</span>, <span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">put \[object\] in/on
\[receptacle\]</span>), receptacle operations
(<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">open/close \[receptacle\]</span>),
and appliance usage (<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.5"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">use \[appliance\]</span>). We use
the standard split with the validation unseen set (134 tasks) for
training and the test unseen set (140 tasks) for evaluation. Success
requires completing the task within 50 steps.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### ScienceWorld.

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

ScienceWorld (Wang<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib18" class="ltx_ref"
title="ScienceWorld: is your agent smarter than a 5th grader?">2022</a>)
is a text-based virtual environment that tests agent reasoning on
elementary school science curricula. The benchmark contains 30 task
types across multiple scientific domains with approximately 11,000 task
variations. For our experiments, we focus on two challenging categories
requiring multi-step reasoning:

- <span id="A2.I2.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Boil (Task
  1-1)</span>: Change the physical state of matter by boiling
  substances, requiring agents to locate heating appliances, transfer
  substances, activate heating, and monitor temperature changes until
  boiling occurs (30 variations).

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I2.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Temperature
  Measurement (Task 2-1)</span>: Use a thermometer to measure unknown
  substance temperatures and classify them into categories based on
  thresholds, requiring systematic search for instruments, focusing
  operations, reading measurements, and decision-making based on
  measured values (540 variations).

  </div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">

These tasks involve procedural knowledge about scientific instruments,
state transitions, and measurement interpretation. Available actions
include navigation, object focusing (<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">focus on \[object\]</span>),
container operations (<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">open/close \[container\]</span>),
appliance activation (<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">activate \[appliance\]</span>), and
observation. Tasks succeed when the scientific goal is achieved (e.g.,
substance reaches boiling state, classification is correct).

</div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### TravelPlanner.

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

TravelPlanner (Xie<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib19" class="ltx_ref"
title="TravelPlanner: a benchmark for real-world planning with language agents">2024</a>)
is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating language agents in tool-use
and complex planning under multiple constraints. Grounded in real-world
travel planning, the benchmark requires agents to formulate multi-day
itineraries including transportation, accommodation, dining, and
attractions while satisfying environment, commonsense, and hard
constraints. The dataset contains 1,225 queries split into:

- <span id="A2.I3.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training
  Set</span>: 45 query-plan pairs with human-annotated reference plans

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I3.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Validation
  Set</span>: 180 queries (20 per constraint configuration group)

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I3.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I3.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Test
  Set</span>: 1,000 queries with random constraint distributions

  </div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">

Constraints are categorized into three types: (1)
<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Environment Constraints</span>
(unavailable transportation/attractions), (2)
<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Commonsense Constraints</span>
(information completeness, activity location consistency,
non-conflicting transportation modes, diverse restaurant/attraction
choices, minimum accommodation stay requirements), and (3)
<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hard
Constraints</span> (budget limits, accommodation rules, room type
preferences, cuisine preferences, transportation restrictions).

</div>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para">

Table <a href="#A2.T5" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 5 ‣ TravelPlanner. ‣ B.1 Dataset Details ‣ Appendix B Details of Experimental Setup ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> summarizes the constraint
distribution in the validation set. Hard constraints appear in
42.78%-35.56% of queries, with house rules being most frequent.
Table <a href="#A2.T6" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 6 ‣ TravelPlanner. ‣ B.1 Dataset Details ‣ Appendix B Details of Experimental Setup ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> details the specific
constraint values, showing diverse combinations (e.g., 5 house rule
types, 7 cuisine categories). Table <a href="#A2.T5" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 5 ‣ TravelPlanner. ‣ B.1 Dataset Details ‣ Appendix B Details of Experimental Setup ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> presents the constraint
quantity distribution: queries are evenly distributed across 0, 1, and 3
constraints (33.33% each), enabling controlled evaluation of planning
complexity.

</div>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p4" class="ltx_para">

Agents access tools including <span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p4.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CitySearch</span>,
<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p4.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FlightSearch</span>,
<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p4.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">AccommodationSearch</span>,
<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p4.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">RestaurantSearch</span>,
<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p4.1.5"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">AttractionSearch</span>, and
<span id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p4.1.6"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GoogleDistanceMatrix</span> to
gather information and construct plans. Success requires satisfying all
specified constraints while maintaining commonsense validity.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Implementation Details

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### LLM Backbone.

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Unless otherwise specified, all methods use Claude-sonnet-4 as the base
LLM with temperature 0.7 for exploration during task execution and
pattern extraction. For the ALFWorld subtask comparison
(Table <a href="#S4.T2" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 2 ‣ Detailed ALFWorld Performance. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), to ensure fair comparison
with prior work, all methods including ours use GPT-4-turbo.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Pattern Retrieval.

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Pattern contexts and task descriptions are embedded using
Qwen3-Embedding-4B (Zhang<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et
al.</span>, <a href="#bib.bib21" class="ltx_ref"
title="Qwen3 embedding: advancing text embedding and reranking through foundation models">2025</a>),
a 4B-parameter multilingual text embedding model supporting 100+
languages with 32k context length. We use an embedding dimension of 1024
for our experiments. The resulting embeddings are stored in
Elasticsearch for efficient retrieval. During retrieval, we employ
Elasticsearch’s Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) algorithm, which combines
keyword-based retrieval via BM25<span id="footnote1"
class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup>1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup>1</sup><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi_BM25"
class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter"
target="_blank">https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi_BM25</a></span></span></span>
and semantic retrieval via cosine similarity. This hybrid approach
balances exact keyword matching with semantic understanding, enabling
robust pattern retrieval across diverse query formulations.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Hyperparameter Configuration.

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

Table <a href="#A2.T7" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 7 ‣ Hyperparameter Configuration. ‣ B.2 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix B Details of Experimental Setup ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> summarizes the key
hyperparameters used in our framework. These values were selected based
on preliminary validation experiments and remained fixed across all
benchmark evaluations. As discussed in Limitations (Appendix), we
acknowledge that optimal settings may vary across domains, and we
provide sensitivity analysis in More Experiments (Appendix) to guide
domain-specific adaptation.

</div>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Baseline Implementation.

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">

To ensure fair comparison, all baseline methods use consistent
experimental settings. The maximum number of action steps per task is
set to 50 across all methods and benchmarks. For
Reflexion (Shinn<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib16" class="ltx_ref"
title="Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning">2023</a>),
we allow a maximum of 3 reflection iterations per task, following the
original paper’s configuration. These settings are synchronized with
prior work including
AutoManual (Chen<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib11" class="ltx_ref"
title="Automanual: constructing instruction manuals by llm agents via interactive environmental learning">2024</a>)
and AutoGuide (Fu<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref"
title="Autoguide: automated generation and selection of context-aware guidelines for large language model agents">2024</a>).
For ATLAS (Choi<span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal"> et al.</span>,
<a href="#bib.bib14" class="ltx_ref"
title="ATLAS: constraints-aware multi-agent collaboration for real-world travel planning">2025</a>)
and AutoGuide, which do not provide open-source implementations, we
directly report results from their papers using the same LLM backbone
when available. All methods use identical task splits and evaluation
metrics to ensure comparable results.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A3" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Additional Experiments

<div id="A3.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Cold-Start Performance with Human-Designed Subagents

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

This experiment tests whether pre-seeding human-designed subagent
patterns can accelerate learning in AutoRefine. This connects to our
main contribution by examining the complementary role of human
expertise: while our framework automatically extracts patterns from
experience, initializing the repository with domain expertise about
constraint priorities could provide immediate performance gains during
the cold-start phase.

</div>

<div id="A3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

We compare two conditions on TravelPlanner validation set (180 tasks):
(1) <span id="A3.SS1.p2.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AutoRefine</span>: standard framework
starting with empty pattern repository, (2) <span id="A3.SS1.p2.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AutoRefine + AttractionPlanner</span>:
framework initialized with a human-designed AttractionPlanner subagent
encoding domain knowledge about attraction planning (daily completeness,
geographic correctness, budget management) before processing any tasks.

</div>

<div id="A3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">

Pre-seeding the AttractionPlanner achieves 7.79% relative improvement in
Final Pass Rate (35.56% $`\rightarrow`$ 38.33%), with the largest gain
in Hard Constraint Macro (+11.42%, from 38.89% to 43.33%)
(Table <a href="#A3.T8" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 8 ‣ C.1 Cold-Start Performance with Human-Designed Subagents ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>). Human expertise about
constraint priorities provides immediate benefits: the pre-seeded
subagent front-loads knowledge about critical constraints (daily
completeness, geographic correctness, data authenticity) that the
baseline system must discover through trial-and-error. The Commonsense
Constraint Micro remains nearly identical (+0.08%), indicating the
human-designed subagent specifically improves hard constraint
satisfaction without disrupting general reasoning. The maintained 100%
Delivery Rate shows the pre-seeded subagent does not introduce
instability.

</div>

</span>Cold-start performance comparison on TravelPlanner validation set
(180 tasks). Pre-seeding with human-designed AttractionPlanner improves
hard constraint satisfaction.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="A3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">

This result validates a hybrid learning strategy: combining human domain
expertise (for immediate constraint satisfaction) with automated
experience extraction (for discovering emergent optimizations and
adapting to edge cases). The pre-seeded subagent encodes explicit
constraint priorities—distinguishing critical constraints (violations
cause plan rejection) from optimization goals (pursued among valid
options)—that enable the system to avoid common failure modes from
task 1. Importantly, the pre-seeded subagent is not static; as
AutoRefine processes tasks, the maintenance mechanism can update the
subagent’s strategy based on utilization statistics and merge it with
extracted skill patterns. This creates a bootstrapping effect: human
expertise provides a robust starting point while automated learning
continues to refine based on actual execution experience.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A3.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

This experiment tests two claims: (1) AutoRefine’s core mechanisms
remain effective across reasonable hyperparameter ranges, and (2)
optimal hyperparameter values are domain-dependent and should be tuned
for deployment.

</div>

<div id="A3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">

We conduct systematic ablations on four critical hyperparameters: (1)
<span id="A3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Batch size
$`K`$</span>, (2) <span id="A3.SS2.p2.2.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pruning percentile $`\alpha`$</span>, (3)
<span id="A3.SS2.p2.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Retrieval count
$`k`$</span>, and (4) <span id="A3.SS2.p2.4.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Similarity threshold $`\theta`$</span>.
For each parameter, we evaluate performance on ALFWorld (validation
unseen set, 134 tasks), ScienceWorld (Task 2-1 temperature measurement,
30 variations), and TravelPlanner (validation set, 180 tasks) while
holding other hyperparameters at default values
(Table <a href="#A2.T7" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 7 ‣ Hyperparameter Configuration. ‣ B.2 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix B Details of Experimental Setup ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). We do not analyze MMR
trade-off $`\lambda`$ and merge threshold $`\theta_{\text{merge}}`$
separately as preliminary experiments show their impact is minimal
within reasonable ranges ($`\lambda\in[0.6,0.8]`$,
$`\theta_{\text{merge}}\in[0.8,0.9]`$).

</div>

<figure id="A3.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="/html/2601.22758/assets/x4.png" id="A3.F4.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="218" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A3.F4.16.8.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span
id="A3.F4.14.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Hyperparameter
sensitivity for batch size <span class="math inline"><em>K</em></span>,
pruning percentile <span class="math inline"><em>α</em></span>, and
retrieval count <span class="math inline"><em>k</em></span>. (a)
ScienceWorld peaks at <span class="math inline"><em>K</em> = 15</span>
while others peak at <span class="math inline"><em>K</em> = 10</span>.
(b) Optimal range <span
class="math inline"><em>α</em> ∈ [15%, 25%]</span> across all
benchmarks. (c) TravelPlanner shows 24% drop at low <span
class="math inline"><em>k</em> = 5</span>. Green shading indicates
optimal ranges.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="A3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">

Figure <a href="#A3.F4" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 4 ‣ C.2 Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> presents the main sensitivity
analysis for K, $`\alpha`$, and k. Across all three parameters, ALFWorld
exhibits relative insensitivity (performance varies within 96-98.5%),
reflecting that simple household tasks are not bottlenecked by pattern
quality.

</div>

<div id="A3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">

In contrast, TravelPlanner shows high sensitivity: batch size $`K`$
variations cause 8-point swings (27.8% at $`K=5`$ to 35.6% at $`K=10`$),
and retrieval count $`k`$ variations cause 9-point swings (26.9% at
$`k=5`$ to 35.6% at $`k=20`$).

</div>

<div id="A3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">

Interestingly, ScienceWorld peaks at $`K=15`$ (71.2%) rather than the
default $`K=10`$ (69.9%), suggesting procedural science tasks benefit
from more contrastive evidence per extraction cycle—likely because
successful temperature measurement requires recognizing subtle
differences in instrument handling across multiple attempts.

</div>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Key Finding: Batch Size Domain-Dependence.

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

The optimal $`K`$ varies by domain: ALFWorld and TravelPlanner peak at
$`K=10`$, while ScienceWorld peaks at $`K=15`$. This difference reflects
task characteristics: ALFWorld’s consistent structure
(search-acquire-deliver) enables pattern learning from fewer examples,
while ScienceWorld’s procedural variations (thermometer location,
substance types) require larger batches to identify generalizable
strategies. TravelPlanner’s sharp performance drop at $`K=5`$ (27.8%,
22% relative decrease from peak) demonstrates insufficient contrastive
evidence—with only 5 tasks, the extraction agent struggles to
distinguish universal constraints (e.g., transportation mode
consistency) from case-specific details.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Key Finding: Pruning Robustness.

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

All benchmarks show consistent optimal range $`\alpha\in[15\%,25\%]`$,
with peaks around 20%: ALFWorld 98.4%, ScienceWorld 70.4%, TravelPlanner
35.6%. The no-pruning condition ($`\alpha=0\%`$) matches our ablation
study’s ”w/o Maintenance” result on TravelPlanner (30.8% vs. 31.1%),
validating experimental consistency. Interestingly, TravelPlanner
degrades more severely without pruning (13.5% relative drop) than with
aggressive pruning at $`\alpha=40\%`$ (10.7% drop), suggesting
accumulated low-quality patterns harm performance more than prematurely
removed useful patterns. This validates our percentile-based design:
removing the bottom 20% adapts to repository quality without absolute
thresholds.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Key Finding: Retrieval Count Sensitivity.

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

TravelPlanner exhibits extreme sensitivity at low $`k`$: $`k=5`$
achieves only 26.9% (24% relative decrease from peak), while ALFWorld
shows minimal impact (97.9%). This pattern reveals task complexity:
TravelPlanner’s multi-subtask structure (transportation, accommodation,
dining, attractions) requires retrieving diverse patterns, whereas
ALFWorld’s focused tasks (find object, apply modifier, deliver) need
fewer patterns. The slight degradation at $`k=30`$ (TravelPlanner:
33.4%) suggests retrieval noise from marginally-relevant patterns,
though the effect is smaller than insufficient retrieval.

</div>

<figure id="A3.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="/html/2601.22758/assets/x5.png" id="A3.F5.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="256" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A3.F5.10.5.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span
id="A3.F5.8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Similarity
threshold <span class="math inline"><em>θ</em></span> analysis. (a)
TravelPlanner peaks at <span class="math inline"><em>θ</em> = 0.6</span>
(36.2%) rather than default <span
class="math inline"><em>θ</em> = 0.5</span> (35.6%), while ALFWorld and
ScienceWorld peak at 0.5. (b) Breakdown shows higher <span
class="math inline"><em>θ</em></span> improves hard constraint
satisfaction (41.3% vs. 38.9%).</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">

Figure <a href="#A3.F5" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 5 ‣ Key Finding: Retrieval Count Sensitivity. ‣ C.2 Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> presents similarity threshold
$`\theta`$ analysis. Surprisingly, TravelPlanner achieves peak
performance at $`\theta=0.6`$ (36.2%) rather than the default
$`\theta=0.5`$ (35.6%), a 1.7% absolute improvement. The breakdown in
Figure <a href="#A3.F5" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 5 ‣ Key Finding: Retrieval Count Sensitivity. ‣ C.2 Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>(b) reveals the cause: higher
threshold improves hard constraint satisfaction (41.3% vs. 38.9% macro
pass rate) by filtering marginally-relevant patterns that introduce
noise. This counter-intuitive finding suggests that for complex domains
with explicit requirements, precision in retrieval outweighs
recall—retrieving 15 highly-relevant patterns is more effective than 20
patterns including 5 marginal ones. ALFWorld and ScienceWorld still peak
at $`\theta=0.5`$, indicating this effect is domain-specific.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="section ltx_paragraph">

##### Parameter Interaction Analysis.

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">

To investigate parameter coupling, we conduct grid searches on
TravelPlanner for three parameter pairs: (1) $`K\times\alpha`$
(extraction vs. maintenance), (2) $`K\times\theta`$ (extraction quality
vs. retrieval strategy), and (3) $`k\times\theta`$ (retrieval count vs.
threshold). Figure <a href="#A3.F6" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 6 ‣ Parameter Interaction Analysis. ‣ C.2 Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> presents the interaction
heatmaps.

</div>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.10.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Extraction-Maintenance
Independence</span> (Figure <a href="#A3.F6" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 6 ‣ Parameter Interaction Analysis. ‣ C.2 Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>a): The $`K\times\alpha`$
heatmap reveals that optimal $`K`$ is relatively independent of
$`\alpha`$. $`K=10`$ consistently outperforms other values across the
entire $`\alpha`$ range (peak 35.6% at $`\alpha=20\%`$), and optimal
$`\alpha=20\%`$ remains consistent across all $`K`$ values. This
validates our framework design: extraction frequency and maintenance
aggressiveness operate on separate mechanisms (pattern creation vs.
quality control) and do not require joint tuning. Only extreme
configurations ($`K=5`$ or $`\alpha=0\%`$) show universal degradation,
confirming both mechanisms are necessary.

</div>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Weak
Extraction-Retrieval Coupling</span>
(Figure <a href="#A3.F6" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 6 ‣ Parameter Interaction Analysis. ‣ C.2 Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>b): The $`K\times\theta`$
heatmap shows weak interaction. Larger $`K`$ (better pattern quality
through more contrastive evidence) exhibits slight preference for higher
$`\theta`$ (0.6 vs. 0.5), suggesting high-quality patterns allow more
aggressive filtering without losing coverage. However, the effect is
modest (1-2% difference), indicating extraction quality does not
strongly constrain retrieval strategy choice.

</div>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p4.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Strong
Retrieval Mechanism Coupling</span>
(Figure <a href="#A3.F6" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 6 ‣ Parameter Interaction Analysis. ‣ C.2 Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiments ‣ AutoRefine: From Trajectories to Reusable Expertise for Continual LLM Agent Refinement"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>c): The $`k\times\theta`$
heatmap reveals strong interaction between retrieval count and
similarity threshold. High $`\theta`$ (0.6-0.7) requires large $`k`$
($`\geq`$<!-- -->20) to compensate for strict filtering and maintain
pattern coverage—$`\theta=0.6`$ with $`k=5`$ achieves only 28.7%, but
$`\theta=0.6`$ with $`k=20`$ reaches 36.2% (peak performance).
Conversely, low $`\theta`$ (0.3-0.4) with large $`k`$ (25-30) introduces
retrieval noise, degrading performance. This demonstrates the
recall-precision tradeoff in retrieval: practitioners should tune $`k`$
and $`\theta`$ jointly rather than independently.

</div>

<figure id="A3.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="/html/2601.22758/assets/x6.png" id="A3.F6.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="285" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span
id="A3.F6.20.10.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure
6</span>: </span><span id="A3.F6.18.9" class="ltx_text"
style="font-size:90%;">Parameter interaction heatmaps on TravelPlanner.
(a) <span class="math inline"><em>K</em> × <em>α</em></span>: Extraction
and maintenance are largely independent (optimal <span
class="math inline"><em>K</em> = 10</span> and <span
class="math inline"><em>α</em> = 20%</span> across ranges). (b) <span
class="math inline"><em>K</em> × <em>θ</em></span>: Weak coupling
(larger <span class="math inline"><em>K</em></span> slightly prefers
higher <span class="math inline"><em>θ</em></span>, 1-2% difference).
(c) <span class="math inline"><em>k</em> × <em>θ</em></span>: Strong
coupling (high <span class="math inline"><em>θ</em></span> requires
large <span class="math inline"><em>k</em></span> to maintain coverage).
Cell values show Final Pass Rate (%).</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p5" class="ltx_para">

These results validate three claims: (1)
<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p5.11.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Robustness</span>: Performance remains
within 3-5% of peak across reasonable ranges ($`K\in[8,15]`$,
$`\alpha\in[15\%,25\%]`$, $`k\in[15,25]`$, $`\theta\in[0.4,0.6]`$); (2)
<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p5.11.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Domain-dependence</span>: Optimal
settings vary—ScienceWorld benefits from larger $`K`$ (15 vs. 10),
TravelPlanner benefits from higher $`\theta`$ (0.6 vs. 0.5); (3)
<span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p5.11.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adaptive design</span>: Percentile-based
pruning ($`\alpha=20\%`$) remains optimal across domains. For
deployment, we recommend: $`K=10`$ (or 15 for procedural tasks),
$`\alpha=20\%`$, $`k=20`$, $`\theta=0.5`$ (or 0.6 for constraint-heavy
tasks) as robust defaults.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A3.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Case Study: Learning Transportation Mode Consistency (100% $`\rightarrow`$ 99.36%)

<div id="A3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A3.SS3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The Case.</span>
In multi-day travel planning, travelers cannot use incompatible
transportation modes on a round trip—driving to a destination but flying
back leaves the vehicle stranded. Formally: if
$`\text{mode}_{\text{outbound}}=\text{self-driving}`$, then
$`\text{mode}_{\text{return}}=\text{self-driving}`$. Despite this
apparent simplicity, baseline methods frequently violate this constraint
by optimizing transportation legs independently (e.g., selecting
self-driving outbound for lower cost, then flight return for speed).

</div>

<div id="A3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">What We
Observe.</span> During execution on TravelPlanner validation set (180
tasks), AutoRefine’s batch contrastive extraction identified
transportation mode conflicts as a high-frequency failure pattern. The
framework automatically extracted a Transportation Coordinator subagent
pattern with three key mechanisms: (1) early return query before
committing to outbound mode, (2) explicit enumeration of 5 compatible
mode pairs (All-Flight, All-Taxi, All-Drive, Fly+Taxi, Taxi+Fly) while
forbidding mixed modes, and (3) pre-output validation of mode
compatibility. After learning, the pattern achieved
<span id="A3.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">100% constraint
satisfaction</span> on validation set re-evaluation (0 violations) and
<span id="A3.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">99.36% on test
set</span> ($`\sim`$<!-- -->1,000 samples, only 7 violations),
demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization across diverse scenarios
(trip durations 3-7 days, 1-3 cities, 150km-2,500km distances, 1-8
travelers, varying budgets).

</div>

<div id="A3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="A3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Why Our Method
Works.</span> Three framework capabilities enabled automatic constraint
learning: (1) <span id="A3.SS3.p3.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Batch contrastive extraction</span>
(every $`K=10`$ tasks) identified transportation conflicts as a
recurring failure by analyzing multiple failures together and
contrasting successful vs. failed plans; (2) <span id="A3.SS3.p3.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Subagent patterns</span> correctly
captured that transportation coordination requires stateful reasoning
and pre-commitment validation—a text guideline like “ensure modes are
consistent” cannot provide the explicit enumeration and constraint
validation needed for reliable enforcement; (3) <span id="A3.SS3.p3.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Merit-based maintenance</span> promoted
high-utility patterns to the core prompt based on retrieval-utilization
statistics, ensuring critical knowledge persisted. This demonstrates
that dual-form patterns capture complex constraint logic and generalize
effectively (99.36% test performance from 180 validation tasks shows
generalizable principles, not overfitting).

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A5" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Pattern Extraction Prompts

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">

This section presents the complete prompts used for extracting and
classifying patterns from task execution trajectories. Our extraction
process consists of three stages: (1) pattern type classification to
determine whether a strategy should be formalized as a skill pattern or
subagent pattern, (2) skill pattern extraction for stateless procedural
knowledge, and (3) subagent pattern extraction for stateful specialized
agents with complete subtask encapsulation.

</div>

<div id="A5.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span>Pattern Classification Prompt

<div id="A5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Before extracting patterns, we first classify whether the observed
successful strategy should be formulated as a skill pattern or a
subagent pattern. This classification is based on formal definitions
from the AutoRefine framework, considering statefulness, reasoning
complexity, subtask completeness, and cognitive load reduction.

</div>

<div id="A5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="A5.SS1.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A5.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>Skill Pattern Extraction Prompt

<div id="A5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

After classifying a strategy as a skill pattern, we extract the
procedural knowledge in either text or code format. This prompt guides
the extraction of stateless, single-purpose strategies from task
execution trajectories.

</div>

<div id="A5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="A5.SS2.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A5.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3 </span>Subagent Pattern Extraction Prompt

<div id="A5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">

After classifying a strategy as a subagent pattern, we extract complete
subagent specifications including system prompts, tool requirements, and
coordination patterns. Our approach supports multi-subagent extraction,
identifying natural decomposition boundaries when complex tasks warrant
multiple specialized agents.

</div>

<div id="A5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="A5.SS3.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span>

</div>

</div>

</div>
